newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr bulls bark, but lack bite so far.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr bulls bark, but lack bite so far.

text.p: The Australian dollar broke a five-day losing streak Wednesday with modest gains but faded far too soon to indicate a reversal in its three-month downtrend.

Demand from local corporates, Swiss and U.S. banks at US$0.7475 caught the market short and squeezed the currency as high as US$0.7520 overnight. Traders said further bids appeared this morning in the hope triggering stops above there, but Tokyo selling of AUD/yen and importer offers pushed it back.
Analysts suspected the market was very short and a bounce to US$0.7560 was possible, but emphasised the longer term outlook remained bearish and a test of US$0.7450 was inevitable.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was making threatening gestures at US$0.7515/20 having crept up from an early US$0.7509/14 and Tuesday's late US$0.7480/85.
This was the first meaningful bounce since the currency collapsed from 76 cents following a shock 40,000 drop in May employment reported last Thursday.

The dire data convinced many the Reserve Bank would cut rates for a fifth time and money rates had moved sharply lower, adding further to the US$'s yield advantage over the A$. For the short term, however, the bank's silence was taken as a sign it would not be moving before its board meeting on July 1.

This assumption had seen 90-day bank bill futures pull back to 94.80 from 94.91 Monday, but this implied the market was pricing in a rate of 5.20 percent compared to the present 5.50 percent cash rate.

Another cut here would take official rates below the U.S. for the first time in almost two decades, although this would be largely symbolic since short term market rates had been well below those in the U.S. since the last RBA easing on May 23.
The outlook was all the more problematic given the expectation the Federal Reserve would have to hike rates sooner or later given the strength of the economy there.
The chance of a hike at the Fed's next meeting on July 1-2 had faded somewhat after inflation data overnight showed CPI rose a benign 0.1 percent in May.

This was not a clear cut positive for the A$, however, since dealers suspected the less chance there was of a U.S. move the greater the risk was of the RBA easing here. Indeed, many reckoned that if the Fed did stand pat at its next meeting the RBA would see it as a window of opportunity for an immedate cut.
A similar argument weighed on would-be A$ bulls in that if the currency itself managed a sustained rally that too would provide room for an easing in policy.
On the crosses activity was more than a little confused after the release of Japanese trade data showing its surplus soared 222 percent to 738.27 billion yen in May.
This was well above median market forecasts of 592 billion but appeared to have been not as bad as some feared since US$/yen rallied in its wake.

The U.S. currency did turn lower when a U.S. official was quoted saying the data reinforced U.S. concerns that Japan's surplus seemed to be rising again. Signs of trade tensions tend to depress the dollar since the market has suspected the U.S. of using currency depreciation as a trade weapon in the past.
The dollar fell as far as 112.80 immediately afterwards but bounced to 113.46/51 at the close to be up on the day.
The local currency followed to stand at 85.27/37, down from a 85.35 high but up on Tuesday's 84.64/74 finish.
In trade weighted terms the dollar edged up to 56.9 from a previous 56.7 close.

There were no domestic data of note due today and little out until May retail trade on July 2. Indeed, analysts felt the most important indicator on the horizon was the Bank of Japan's June Tankan survey on June 25 which could decide if rates there were heading higher. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
